synopsis: Two autonomous-haulage collisions in Western Australia in 2019 are presented as evidence of communications and traction failures rather than perception failures [f1371]. At Fortescue’s Christmas Creek mine, an autonomous truck reversed into a stationary truck on 11 February 2019; at BHP’s Jimblebar mine, the regulator attributed a collision to an unloaded truck losing traction in bad weather and sliding into a loaded truck’s path [f1372, f1375]. A Western Australian incident report also documents mode misunderstanding and desensitization around autonomous haul trucks, adding a human-factors concern [f10445]. The mines regulator, DMIRS, now DEMIRS, followed up the Fortescue and BHP collisions, while evidence acceptance for the Komatsu FrontRunner case is attributed to the mine operator [f15546, f1830]. The glossary says Australian state mining regulators, including Western Australia’s, do not mandate automatic braking, but explicitly notes that the booklet did not verify DMIRS/DEMIRS codes, limiting confidence in that regulatory conclusion [f15525, f15547].

relations.note: Jimblebar's reported traction loss supports the non-perception failure conclusion.
